norms.what: The skill runs as a slash command with an optional path. Asking about scope before any work costs a round trip on the one decision a user rarely wants to make; stating the assumption in the report keeps it visible and correctable. In 0.3.0 the root is stated in the plan shown before any reading ([N07]) instead of at the top of the report, because the plan is now the first thing the user sees and the place where scope is confirmed.

These are the surfaces Claude Code reads instructions from: the memory files and their `@path` imports, path-scoped rules, subagent definitions, skills, commands and settings. API code is included because four of the Opus 5.5 breaking changes live in request code rather than in prose. In 0.3.0 the directories are narrowed to their Markdown files and the API search to code files and a `thinking` request parameter: in a test on a small project, searching every file for the word "thinking" returned prose about thinking, not API calls, and in a large harness with ~430 instruction files the JSON and YAML beside the skills were counted as instruction text.

`rg` skips hidden entries while traversing, so a sweep from `.` walks past `.claude/`, where most of a Claude Code setup lives, and exits 0 with zero hits, which reads as a clean audit. Naming the directory, or passing `--hidden`, is what makes the search reach it.

Instruction trees are often materialised by a tool — a plugin install, a sync script, a shared package — and gitignored in the project that receives them. An edit there is silently discarded by the next install, or, through a symlink, changes another project. Reporting the change for its source keeps it from being lost. In 0.3.0 it also says how to count a symlink that stays inside the root: in the small-project test a `CLAUDE.md` linked to `AGENTS.md` was listed and measured twice. It is now listed once, under its real path, with the link named beside it. In 0.3.1 `.claude/settings.local.json` is exempt: Claude Code keeps it gitignored by design, and [N48] offers it as the personal destination for the project's model and effort.

A mature setup can hold hundreds of instruction files. Reading all of them at once fills the context window and dilutes attention on each file, which is where an audit loses findings. Measuring first costs one command and decides everything after it. Bytes divided by four is a deliberately rough estimate: it only has to size batches, not bill anyone. In 0.3.0 the estimate became a token range from bytes/4 to three times that: on the large harness, per-file reading overhead reached about 2.8× the bytes/4 figure, and the whole run spent ~2.99M tokens across subagents and the main session. A single figure read as a promise; a range with the multiplier stated does not. Cost is stated in tokens, because the session cannot know how the user is billed. In 0.3.1 the range adds the skill's own fixed cost and labels the figure an estimate: in a 0.3.0 run on a small project that fit one batch, the audit added about 12,000 tokens of context, three to five times the top of the range, because the range counted only the files. The measure also sizes the excluded groups, since [N36] asks for their size in the plan and 0.3.0 gave no command for it. In 0.4.0 the fixed cost is recalibrated to about 30,000–40,000 tokens and kept apart from the stage's marginal cost: in the final test of 0.3.1 on a small project (2 instruction files, 1 batch, ~1.3k tokens read, ~33.5k tokens of context measured), the fixed part came to about 32,000 tokens, some 2.7× the 12,000 figure, because the skill's body, the skill list and reminders the session injects, and the round trips of its questions all count. The range runs above that measurement because the 0.4.0 SKILL.md is larger. The norm names what the figure covers so the user can judge it. In 0.4.1 every figure is labelled "tokens of context (estimate)": in the test of 0.4.0 on a small project (20 model calls, 37.8k tokens of context growth and 1.5M tokens read from cache), a figure labelled only "tokens" read as the amount billed, which counts the context again on every round trip. In 0.4.2 the fixed cost also measures the project memory the session loaded — `CLAUDE.md`, `CLAUDE.local.md` and `AGENTS.md` with their `@path` imports, as bytes/4 — and shows it summed with the skill's own, as in "fixed: ~30–40k from the skill + ~38k from the project memory": in a test of 0.4.1 on a large harness the real fixed cost was ~118k against the 30–40k announced, because the project's memory, loaded before the skill ran, was not counted.

The batch ceiling keeps each audited slice small beside a 1M-token window, so the pattern table and the batch both sit in focus. Grouping by relationship keeps an import and the file importing it in the same view, which is where a contradiction between them shows. In 0.3.0 it adds that each line range must fit one read: on the large harness a file bigger than one batch still exceeded the Read tool's per-call limit when read as a single range. In 0.3.1 a group that belongs together but exceeds one batch — a `CLAUDE.md` with its imports — is split into consecutive batches and the plan says so: in a 0.3.0 run on a large harness with ~430 instruction files, such a group was larger than one batch, and the norm said to keep it together without saying what to do when it could not fit.

A long audit that says nothing reads as stuck. A one-line statement of intent before the work starts is the update cadence the Opus 5.5 guide recommends for human-in-the-loop runs. In 0.3.0 the statement became a full plan: the checklist, root, file count by area, exclusions, git state, batch count, cost range and run mode. In the large-harness test, the one-line statement was the only thing shown before ~2.8M tokens were spent across 47 batches, and the user saw no cost or alternative until the run was over. The plan feeds the cost and scope gate in [N39]. In 0.4.0 the plan is a short message that leads into the [N39] question, and the excluded groups are named "not audited" per [N36]. In 0.4.2 the plan shows two Markdown tables, translated per [N34]: one by area, with a row for what is not audited, its total and the reason, and one by option, with the recommendation marked ★, the reason below it, and a footnote with the fixed cost. The maintainer asked for tables so the areas and options can be compared at a glance. Batch counts read "~N or more" because they are a floor: grouping files per [N06] packs fewer tokens into each batch than the bytes/4 total implies, and in a test of 0.4.1 an estimate of 18 batches came to 22.

Writing findings to disk after each batch turns the audit into a sequence of small, focused passes whose results survive context compaction, and lets the report be built from the file rather than from memory of earlier batches. In 0.3.1 each batch is written under a line naming it, clean batches included, so a resumed run ([N47]) can tell which batches are done.

One line per finding with a location, a pattern id and a quote is what the report groups and counts, and what a later re-scan compares against. A dated path keeps a second audit from overwriting the first.

Several rows apply only to one kind of project — chat, unattended agents, API code. Recording a row's signal where its condition does not hold produces findings the user has to argue away, which is the fastest way to make an audit unreadable. In 0.3.0 it adds that a file pinned to a model other than Opus 5 or 5.5 gets no finding from a model-behavior row: on the large harness, P03, P04, P06, P07 and P09 carried no model qualifier and matched agents pinned to other models, whose behavior the Opus 5.5 guide says nothing about. In 0.4.0 P01 resolves model aliases as the Claude Code model-config page states: `opus`, `opus[1m]` and `default` are Opus 5.5 on the Anthropic API, Claude Platform on AWS, Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud, other models on Microsoft Foundry, and `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL` overrides `opus`. The final test of 0.3.1 on a small project (2 instruction files, 1 batch, ~1.3k tokens read, ~33.5k tokens of context measured) found that P01 had no rule for a model named by alias, so whether such a project runs on Opus 5.5 was left to guesswork.

The skill was narrowed to one transition so that every proposed change rests on one guide. Verification steps, delegation prompts and severity filters became outdated with Opus 5, not 5.5; they are still worth knowing about, so they are listed, and left to an audit whose evidence covers them.

A model upgrade changes how instructions about model behavior land; it changes nothing about a project's facts or its safety boundaries. An audit that removes a confirmation step because it looks redundant does real damage, so those classes are protected by rule rather than by judgment.

norms.where: Stage 3 — Report: explain it in the chat
norms.what: A large setup produces more findings than a chat message holds. A file keeps the whole report reviewable, shareable and diffable, and gives Stage 5 a place to record what was applied. In 0.3.0 the file also lists what [N36] excluded, and it is no longer the only place the user reads the report: the chat carries it per [N15], and the file keeps the full record. In 0.4.0 the report file takes everything the chat leaves out per [N15] — coverage, what was not audited, older residue, counts by confidence, and every empty section written as "none" — plus the trail of approved gates from [N50]. In 0.4.1 the opening points to the decision section that holds the gates approved after Stage 3, per [N50], since the opening is written before those gates exist and the trail must read as one.

Where the session can publish a page, a report is easier to read and to share with a team there than in a file inside the repository. It is conditional because the tool exists only in some Claude environments. In 0.3.0 the artifact stopped being automatic and moved to the close, as an offer the user accepts or declines. In the small-project test, publishing it cost ~12k of the run's ~28k tokens for a report with one finding, and the detour broke the flow between the report and the question; the maintainer asked for it to be offered at most.

norms.where: Stage 3 — Report: explain it in the chat
norms.what: The chat summary exists to support the decision in Stage 4, not to replace the report. In 0.3.0 the chat summary became the report itself, in a fixed form rendered as Markdown: a numbered table of changes with a type and a confidence, one plain-language line of why per pattern, and the sections that change nothing, shown as "none" when empty. Both tests showed that counts plus five findings, with the rest in a file, did not let the user decide from the chat; the maintainer asked for a structured report in the chat, with fixed sections, that explains rather than points elsewhere. The type column is what [N43] groups by, and the fifteen-row cap keeps a large setup readable. In 0.4.0 the chat report was cut to what a decision needs, in a fixed order: one summary line, the numbered table, one line of why per pattern, one aggregated line for the categories with items that change nothing, and the migrate line only when there is API code. In the final test of 0.3.1 on a small project (2 instruction files, 1 batch, ~1.3k tokens read, ~33.5k tokens of context measured), headings followed by "- none" were unreadable in the terminal, because each "none" seemed to belong to the heading below it; and coverage, older residue and counts by confidence pushed the table and the question apart. The maintainer set the principle stated at the top of the skill: the chat carries progress and decisions, and reference material goes to the report and the close.

norms.where: Stage 3 — Report: explain it in the chat
norms.what: The first version proposed a full diff in the report. A diff for every finding is expensive to produce and mostly discarded once the user chooses a subset, so it is written only for what was approved.

Which changes to make is the user's decision. A question with options is answered in one step, where a list of decisions inside a long report has to be found first. The recommendation is bounded so the skill never recommends applying a change the guide does not state. In 0.3.0 the options changed from high-confidence-only to: every proposed change with its count by confidence, choose by type (offered only when more than one type is present), diff first, or stop; and the recommendation adapts to the findings. In the small-project test the only finding was medium confidence, so "apply every high-confidence change" was an empty option and the rule for recommending it was vacuously true. Choosing by pattern id meant nothing to a user who had not read the table; choosing by type of action (remove, add, setting, rewrite) does. The dirty-tree warning from [N19] now sits in the option descriptions, so no separate question is needed before editing. In 0.3.1 a P01 row adds the destination question from [N48] to the same call, so the user decides what to apply and where the project's model and effort go in one step. In 0.4.0 each applying option carries the estimated cost of applying it and the total expected, per [N49]. In 0.4.1 the applying estimate adds about 5,000 tokens for the verification and the close to the size of the edits: in the test of 0.4.0 on a small project the applying option announced 1–2k tokens and applying took about 5.6k, because re-scanning the edited files, recording each change and closing the run cost more than the edits themselves.

Headless runs (`claude -p`, CI) have no interactive question tool. Changing nothing there keeps an unattended run from editing a project without approval. In 0.3.0 the fallback for a missing `AskUserQuestion` moved to [N33], which covers every question in the run; this norm now covers only runs where no one can answer, and ends them through the same close ([N45]) as every other path, since in the small-project test the stop path had no defined ending.

Mixing an audit's edits into uncommitted work makes both hard to review and impossible to revert separately. In 0.3.0 the check moved from the start of Stage 5 to the plan: the user sees the tree state before choosing anything, and a dirty tree becomes a note in the applying options of [N17] instead of one more question after the decision.

The approval covers a specific set of changes. Applying more than that, even an obviously good change, turns the approval into a blank check. Files marked read-only in Stage 1 are reported for their source instead, per [N04].

One of the Stage 4 options is to review the diff first; this norm is what makes that option mean something. In 0.3.0 the diff is shown without editing any file and is followed by a question: apply all, choose by type, or stop. In the small-project test the diff-first path had no defined continuation. In 0.4.0 the question after the diff is a cost gate per [N49], like the one in [N17].
An edit can leave a pattern in place — a removed sentence repeated elsewhere in the same file — or remove more than intended. The re-scan checks both, against the same table the audit used.

The Opus 5.5 guide recommends testing several effort levels against the project's own evals rather than carrying settings over. The audit applies documented guidance; only the project's measurements show it holds for that project. In 0.3.0 it applies only where the audit ran: a run cancelled at the plan has nothing to measure.

A report that records only findings cannot answer, a month later, which of them were acted on. In 0.3.0 the decision itself is recorded too, so a report where the user chose to stop still says so. In 0.3.1 the decision is written before the first edit and each change as it is applied, not all at the end: a 0.3.0 run on a small project lost its API connection mid-run, and a record written only at the end cannot say which edits were already made. In 0.4.1 the decision section also records the gates approved after Stage 3, per [N50].

The Opus 5.5 migration guide itself recommends `/claude-api migrate this project to claude-opus-5-5`, which swaps model IDs, rewrites the breaking parameters in eight SDK languages and adjusts for platform-specific IDs and features. Editing request code here would duplicate that work with less coverage, and would break this skill's own ask-before-edit contract only to reach a result the official skill already delivers. The four breaking-change rows stay in the table so the report still shows them, but their fix is the hand-off. Running the official skill from inside this one was rejected: its `migrate` edits once the scope is confirmed, which contradicts Stage 4, and this skill must also work where `claude-api` is not installed.

Adapted from the keep list of Anthropic's prompt-audit guidance, which separates trigger text from behavioral text: a skill's description decides whether it is invoked at all, and skills tend to under-trigger, so urgency there can be deliberate. A grep cannot tell the two apart, so the norm classifies by function before a finding is recorded.

N09 asked for a confidence level without defining one, so two runs could grade the same finding differently. The scale follows the prompt-audit rubric (documented or erroring = high, observed behavior = medium, inference = low), restated in terms of the Opus 5.5 guide's own wording: it states some changes, and only asks the reader to consider or re-test others. In 0.3.0 the high grade also covers the Claude Code documentation: the small-project test could not grade a P01 finding, because the Opus 5.5 guide alone does not say which settings Claude Code reads for effort, while the Claude Code model-config page states it. In 0.4.0 P01's own confidence rule is made precise: high only when the project sets neither `model` nor `effortLevel` and the user relies on a top-level `effortLevel` in their user settings, which Opus 5.5 ignores. In the final test of 0.3.1 on a small project (2 instruction files, 1 batch, ~1.3k tokens read, ~33.5k tokens of context measured), the 0.3.1 wording, "the user's settings hold only that ignored key", could be read two ways.

From prompt-audit's prime directive: an audit that finds nothing should change nothing. A report with no findings reads as a failed run, which pressures the auditor to stretch a row; stating that a clean result is valid removes that pressure.

norms.where: Stage 3 — Report: explain it in the chat
norms.what: N11 and N25 both leave findings unaddressed by design. Without a named next step the report ends at a dead end; with one, the reader knows which tool covers the rest. `prompt-audit` is a public subcommand of Anthropic's claude-api skill for dated patterns across model generations, and `migrate` handles request code. In 0.4.0 both closing lines live in the report file; the chat shows the migrate line only when there is API code, and the prompt-audit pointer goes to the close in [N45].

Adapted from prompt-audit's verification step: tests, hooks, log parsers and gate scripts sometimes match on instruction text, so a removal that looks safe in the instruction file can break a check elsewhere. N22 re-scans only the edited files and cannot see such a dependency. In 0.3.0 the dependency is named in the closing message, since the user now reads the outcome in the chat.

A test run against a large, already-migrated instruction corpus showed that N12 guards only against proposing removals: the audit would have re-proposed an elapsed-time signal (P12) the project had evaluated and declined with a cited reason, and could not tell an Opus 5 instruction carried over unexamined from one re-tested and kept on purpose (P07). The same run led to narrowing P01 to files that run on Opus 5 or 5.5, since agents pinned to other models carry their own effort settings, and to exempting P09 where a file points to centrally stated update guidance. In 0.3.0 it uses the evaluation [N38] searches for in Stage 1, records a project-wide decision once instead of once per file, and takes precedence over older residue: on the large harness five findings were already decided, one decision was repeated per file, and the auditor could not tell whether [N11] or this norm applied.

Added in 0.3.0. In the small-project test the user lost track of the run three times: after the report, when the question had no usable high-confidence option, and after choosing to stop. A checklist shown first and reprinted at every stage answers "where are we and what is next" without a question. It is plain text because task-list tools are not present in every session, and the `[-]` mark lets a cancelled or headless run end with an honest list.

Added in 0.3.0. The maintainer asked for every decision to go through `AskUserQuestion`, which the user answers in one step, with the recommendation first. Without the tool — a headless run, or a client that lacks it — a numbered question in the chat keeps the same options and the same rule that nothing changes until the user answers. The small-project test exercised this fallback and it worked.

Added in 0.3.0. In the small-project test the report came out in English and the artifact in Portuguese in the same run, because nothing said which language to use. Quoted text, paths, ids and commands stay untouched so a finding can still be found with a search. In 0.3.1 the two files under `.claude/audits/` follow the user's language too, with the template headings translated: a 0.3.0 run on a small project wrote the chat in Portuguese and both files in English, because the norm named only the chat and the report. In 0.4.2 the norm names every file under `.claude/audits/`, including the brief shared with subagents per [N40]: "both files" left that brief out, so it could come out in English in a run held in another language.

Added in 0.3.0. The large-harness test ran 47 batches over ~41 minutes; without a line per batch the run looked stuck. One line per batch or subagent, with done-of-total and findings added, is the short recap cadence the Opus 5.5 guide recommends for long human-in-the-loop work. In 0.3.1 progress is counted in batches, not subagents: in a 0.3.0 run on a large harness with ~430 instruction files, one subagent covered several batches, and "subagent 2 of 8" said nothing about how much of the audit was done.

Added in 0.3.0. In the large-harness test, 427 files were listed and ~1.3M of ~2.57M estimated tokens were JSON sidecars; vendored references and data files were queued as if they were instructions. After exclusion 246 files remained. Naming each excluded group with its size keeps the exclusion visible and reversible. In 0.4.0 the groups are named "Not audited (not instructions for the model)": in the final test of 0.3.1 on a small project (2 instruction files, 1 batch, ~1.3k tokens read, ~33.5k tokens of context measured), the maintainer read "excluded" as files the audit would delete.

Added in 0.3.0. Whether Opus 5.5 has an effort level depends on the user's settings file, which lies outside the audit root: a top-level `effortLevel` there does not count for Opus 5.5, while a level saved for it under `modelSettings` does. The small-project test reported P01 without knowing this, which made it a likely false positive. Reading the file as context, and never editing it, closes the gap without widening the audit's scope. In 0.3.1 the user's settings are context for the explanation of P01, never a file to edit: P01 now writes to the project, and what the user's own `effortLevel` does today is part of why. In 0.4.1 P01 cites https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config#adjust-effort-level on its own row, inside the statement that a top-level `effortLevel` in `~/.claude/settings.json` does not count for Opus 5.5, and its "applies when" says that such a key does not count as an effort already set. The page says a top-level `effortLevel` in the user settings file doesn't count for Opus 5.5, while one in project, local or managed settings applies to every model. In the test of 0.4.0 on a small project the claim was correct but its source sat only in [N48] and the Sources section, far from the row it supports. In 0.4.2 P01 counts a level saved per model as already set: `/effort` and the `/model` picker save it under `modelSettings["claude-opus-5-5"]` in the user's settings, and the Claude Code docs say each model keeps its own saved level. 0.4.1 would have recommended setting an effort a user had already saved for Opus 5.5.

Added in 0.3.0. [N31] depends on knowing where the project records its Opus 5.5 decisions, and nothing told the auditor to look for that record. In the large-harness test five findings turned out to be already decided. Searching for the record in Stage 1 makes it available to every batch. In 0.3.1 the search also covers decision records outside the inventory, such as `docs/adrs/`, `docs/**/decisions/` and `docs/audits/`: in a 0.3.0 run on a large harness with ~430 instruction files, the audit stated that no record called a model pin deliberate when one existed under `docs/audits/`, the user approved a change on that false premise, and only the text-dependency check in [N30] caught it, by chance. In 0.4.0 the search also reads the project's auto memory, which Claude Code keeps outside the root under `~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/` unless `autoMemoryDirectory` moves it. The final test of 0.3.1 on a small project (2 instruction files, 1 batch, ~1.3k tokens read, ~33.5k tokens of context measured) showed that a project's decisions can live there as well as in the repository. It is read as context only, never edited. In 0.4.1 the auto memory is read from the main checkout's key when the session runs in a git worktree: Claude Code keys a project's memory by the main repository, so `~/.claude/projects/<worktree key>/memory/` is not where the project's memory lives. In the test of 0.4.0 on a small project the run looked under the worktree's key. `git rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-common-dir` names the main checkout's `.git` directory, whose parent is the checkout.

Added in 0.3.0. In the large-harness test the run spent ~2.8M tokens in subagents before the user saw any cost; the maintainer asked for a gate that shows the cost and lets the user continue, reduce the scope, use subagents, or cancel. Subagents are an option, never the default: they finish sooner, but each one reads the pattern table and the norms again, so they cost as much or more. The ten-batch threshold for recommending the in-session run is a judgment call from the two tests: the small project fit one batch, and the harness's 47 batches were well past what one session reads comfortably. A setup that fits one batch skips the question, since there is nothing to trade off. In 0.3.1 the subagent option carries its own estimate: in a 0.3.0 run on a large harness with ~430 instruction files, each subagent loaded the project's memory with its imports (~38,000 tokens) plus the rules injected with it before reading a single file, and the run went ~1.9× past the top of the range that "about the same or more" had implied. The reduced-scope option now warns that it leaves out the skills, which is where that test found most of the text tuned for Opus 5. In 0.4.0 the question is asked even for a single batch, and it names what will be read, the stage's marginal cost and the total expected. The maintainer asked for it explicitly: one more question on a small project is the price of answering "the skill spends too many tokens" with "every spend was shown and approved". The reduced scope is offered only when it saves a batch, and subagents only when there is more than one batch, each with its extra cost stated per subagent. In 0.4.2 the gate is one question offering the pertinent combinations of scope and run mode — full or reduced, in this session or in subagents — plus the quick sweep of [N51] and cancel, each combination offered only when it makes sense: subagents only with more than one batch, the reduced scope only when it reduces. The maintainer closed this decision so that one question carries every choice the plan offers, instead of a second question from [N46] after the reduced scope. The subagent options state their tier per [N40], so their cost is the cost at that tier. `AskUserQuestion` takes at most four options per question, so a gate with more pertinent options falls back to [N33]'s numbered list rather than dropping one. In 0.4.3 the subagent options state that they run on Opus 5.5 at `medium` effort, the tier [N40]'s agent pins, with the cost at that tier, and they are offered only when that agent is available; otherwise the question says why and offers the in-session options only. The same release drops the project memory from each subagent's base cost, since the agent sets `omitClaudeMd`; on Claude Code older than v2.1.271, which ignores that field, the memory is still counted.

Added in 0.3.0. In the large-harness test the subagents were refused the Write tool and one worked around it with a shell heredoc, so findings landed in inconsistent places. Having each subagent return its findings as text in the [N09] line format, and letting only this session write the file, keeps one writer and one format. In 0.3.1 the shared material can go in one file under `.claude/audits/` that each subagent reads instead of being pasted inline into every prompt, a need found in a 0.3.0 run on a large harness with ~430 instruction files; it also names the project facts a subagent needs to apply [N31], [N10] and [N20] — the Opus 5.5 evaluation, model pins and read-only files. Subagents still write no findings. In 0.4.0 subagents start only after their own cost was approved per [N49]. In 0.4.2 each subagent runs on an explicit, cheaper tier passed as `model` in the call, such as `sonnet`, instead of inheriting the session's model: classifying files against a closed pattern table needs no more, and the per-invocation `model` parameter comes first in the order Claude Code resolves a subagent's model. The maintainer closed this decision; inheriting the session's model runs every subagent on the session's tier, usually the most expensive one. The norm also defers to the project's own dispatch conventions, since some harnesses enforce a brief format or required fields through `CLAUDE.md` or hooks. In 0.4.3 the subagents are always `inbrace-config:batch-auditor`, an agent this plugin ships with `model: claude-opus-5-5`, `effort: medium` and `tools: Read, Grep, Glob`, and the call passes no `model`. The maintainer closed this decision after a test on a large harness where the `sonnet` subagents got two classifications wrong that needed judgment: one marked as older residue a filter the project had already decided on, and another proposed a P12 by inference; the main session had to correct both. The Agent tool call accepts `model` but not effort, so a `general-purpose` subagent inherits the session's effort; an agent definition sets both, and the plugin components page lists `model`, `effort` and `tools` among the fields a plugin agent supports, while it ignores `permissionMode`, `hooks`, `mcpServers` and `initialPrompt`. Passing `model` in the call would override the agent's pin, since the per-invocation parameter comes first in the subagent model order. The read-only tool list enforces what the norm already required: findings come back as text and this session is the only writer. Where the agent is not listed, or the project forbids it, the run uses no subagents and [N39] offers only the in-session options. The agent also sets `omitClaudeMd: true`, after review of the pull request: in the large-harness test each subagent loaded the project memory, ~38,000 tokens of `CLAUDE.md` with its imports, and re-read it on every round trip, while it only classifies the files it reads with Read and the brief already carries the project facts it needs. The sub-agents page says the field launches a subagent with only the managed policy files of the `CLAUDE.md` hierarchy — no user, project or local `CLAUDE.md`, project rules or `AGENTS.md` — and requires Claude Code v2.1.271 or later; a `CLAUDE.md` that falls in a batch is still audited, since the subagent reads it as a file.

Added in 0.3.0. The lexical signals of P07 and P09–P12 — scope, delegation, checklist — matched project prose about pull requests, architecture and runbooks. In the large-harness test those false positives dominated the audit's cost, while 41 of 47 batches ended clean. The norm filters by function before a finding is recorded.

Added in 0.3.0. The report carries items this skill never edits: re-test notes, already-decided items, unclear ones, API code handed off to `/claude-api migrate`, and older residue. Counting them under "every proposed change" would inflate the option and suggest the skill edits them.

Added in 0.3.0. The maintainer chose type of action as the grouping for a partial approval, because a user can decide on "remove" or "setting" without learning the pattern ids. Listing only the types present, with the table numbers each one covers, keeps the multi-select question short and tied to the table the user just read. In 0.3.1 the setting type names what it now covers — the project's model and effort (P01) and a model pin (P20) — and a P01 row goes to the file chosen per [N48]. P21 is not a setting: an agent or skill without `effort:` inherits the session's level, so with P01 applied it already runs at `medium`, and a finding there was noise. P21 now flags only an `effort:` carried over from Opus 5 onto a file pinned to Opus 5.5, as a re-test item with no edit, since Opus 5.5's `medium` matches or beats Opus 5 at `high`.
Added in 0.3.0. In the small-project test the question was asked even when its applying option was empty. With an empty table nothing can be decided, so the run goes straight to the close.

Added in 0.3.0. In the small-project test the stop path ended with no closing message, and the report files under `.claude/audits/` were left untracked without a word. Every path — cancelled at the plan, stopped at the report, headless, or applied — now ends with the same close: the final checklist, what was and was not applied, what to do with the report files, and one next step. In 0.4.0 the close also carries the reference material the chat report leaves out per [N15], listing only what has items. In 0.4.2 the close adds one line on checking the cost: the gates estimate tokens of context, while `subagent_tokens`, the statusline and the bill add the cache re-reads of every round trip, so they run higher. Without that line, the harness's larger figures read as a wrong estimate.

Added in 0.3.0, after review of the pull request. The reduced scope that [N39] recommends above ten batches is estimated on its own, and in a very large setup its plan can still exceed ten batches. Without a second gate, choosing it would start a run whose cost the user had not seen. Asking again with the new plan keeps the rule that no reading starts before the user sees what it will cost; reducing again is not offered, since the reduced scope is already the smallest one the skill defines. In 0.3.1 it names the recommendation, which 0.3.0 left open: this session up to ten batches, subagents above that with their extra cost stated, as measured in a 0.3.0 run on a large harness with ~430 instruction files. In 0.4.2 the second question is retired and its content absorbed into the single [N39] question, where the reduced scope in subagents is now an option of its own; the id is kept, as ids are never reused, and its text now states the recommendation rule, which carries 0.3.1's over: this session up to ten batches, the reduced scope above that, in subagents when it still has more than ten. The quick sweep of [N51] is never recommended with ten batches or fewer, since it misses the patterns that need context, which a full read of that size can afford. In 0.4.3 the subagent recommendation applies only when [N40]'s agent is available, since [N39] offers no subagents otherwise.

Added in 0.3.1. A 0.3.0 run on a small project lost its API connection in the middle of Stage 5; on resuming, nothing said which stage it was in or which edits were made, so the run could repeat an edit or skip one. The findings file ([N08]) and the report file ([N24]) are already on disk and now record each finished batch and each applied edit, so they are enough to find the point to continue from.

Added in 0.3.1, with the rewrite of P01. In a 0.3.0 run on a small project, the fix for P01 wrote `effortLevel` into the shared project settings without saying that this imposes the level on every contributor, and the value `medium` was the auditor's inference. The maintainer decided the skill recommends Opus 5.5 at `medium` — the Opus 5.5 guide says its `medium` matches or beats Opus 5 at `high`, at lower cost — and that the user chooses where it applies: shared settings, recommended so the whole team gets the same model and effort, or local settings for one person. The Claude Code docs are cited because they state the rule the choice depends on: a top-level `effortLevel` in project settings applies to every model, while one in the user's settings does not count for Opus 5.5. In 0.4.1 the shared option stays recommended, but when the repository has a public remote — checked with `gh repo view --json visibility` or an equivalent, and reported as unknown when it cannot be determined — the option warns that it fixes Opus 5.5 at `medium` for every contributor who opens the project. For a public repository that audience is anyone who clones it, which the recommendation did not say.

Added in 0.4.0. After the final test of 0.3.1 on a small project (2 instruction files, 1 batch, ~1.3k tokens read, ~33.5k tokens of context measured), the maintainer wanted every spend visible and approved before it happens, so that the answer to "the skill spends too many tokens" is that each spend was shown and approved. The gates sit where the cost is: reading the batches, applying changes, and starting subagents. Separating the fixed cost, already paid once the skill loads, from each step's marginal cost keeps the question about what the user can still decide. There is no minimum size: a single-batch run is asked too. In 0.4.1 each figure is labelled "tokens of context (estimate)", and the first gate says in one sentence that the billed tokens run higher because every round trip re-reads the context, mostly from cache at a discount: the test of 0.4.0 on a small project measured 20 model calls, 37.8k tokens of context growth and 1.5M tokens read from cache, so the context estimate and the billed total differ by more than an order of magnitude.

Added in 0.4.0. A gate approved in the chat is lost once the session ends. Writing each one with the estimate shown into the report file leaves an audit trail that shows what was spent and that the user approved it. In 0.4.1 the gates approved after Stage 3 — the [N17] and [N48] answers and applying changes — go into the decision section [N24] appends, and the top of the report points to it: in the test of 0.4.0 on a small project the top of the report was written before those gates were approved, so the trail was split between the opening and the decision section.

Added in 0.4.2. The maintainer made the quick sweep — searching for the table's signals and reading only the lines around each match — an official option with a stated limit, for setups too large to read in full. The cost of about 50,000–150,000 tokens of context is the maintainer's estimate. The limit follows from how the rows are written: P01–P06 and P14–P20 have a lexical signal a search finds, while P07 and P09–P12 depend on what a file does as a whole — tuning written for Opus 5, missing cadences, unattended or multi-agent runs — which a few lines around a match cannot show.

Added in 0.4.2. An option the skill does not define has no estimate the skill stands behind and no stated limit, so the maintainer made the set of options closed: every gate offers only what the skill defines, and a missing option is added here, with its cost and limit, rather than invented in a run.
